content: The primary audience for this guideline includes health workers who provide services to students in primary and secondary educational institutions. Secondary audiences encompass academics, school health implementers (such as school health workers), other school staff (including managers, administrators, and teachers), and students themselves. A health worker is defined as an individual whose primary role is to deliver health promotion, prevention, care, and/or treatment services, such as a nurse or clinical psychologist, but not a teacher. School Health Services (SHS) are provided by health workers to students enrolled in primary or secondary education, either on school premises or in external health service facilities that have formal agreements with schools to deliver health services to their students. The guideline does not address aspects of health-promoting schools (HPS) that do not involve health workers, such as health education delivered by teachers in classrooms. It also does not propose a universal approach to SHS, recognizing the diversity of delivery systems, such as school-based versus school-linked services, or the use of multidisciplinary health worker teams versus a single cadre of health workers. The guideline does not provide specific recommendations on the content or delivery of SHS, as these depend on the context, available resources, and the broader health system. This guideline is part of a series of global guidance documents on school health, including SHS programming and implementation. It aims to contribute to achieving specific Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) targets, such as ending epidemics of AIDS, tuberculosis, malaria, and neglected tropical diseases; combating hepatitis, waterborne diseases, and other communicable diseases; reducing premature mortality from noncommunicable diseases through prevention, treatment, and mental health promotion; strengthening substance abuse prevention and treatment; achieving universal health coverage (SDG 3); and eliminating violence against women and girls, harmful practices, and ensuring universal access to sexual and reproductive health and rights (SDG 5). A Steering Group was established to provide technical support for the guideline development process. This group, led by the WHO Department of Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health and Ageing, included representatives from other relevant WHO departments, regional offices, and UNESCO. The Steering Group proposed experts with technical knowledge in school health and expertise in evidence review and synthesis to join the Guideline Development Group (GDG). The GDG comprised academics, public health professionals, and clinicians with multidisciplinary expertise in school, adolescent, and child health. To comply with WHO’s Conflict of Interest Policy, declarations of interest (DoI) were requested from all GDG members, experts, and external partners involved in the evidence review, guideline development, and drafting processes. The Steering Group reviewed these declarations and found no significant conflicts of interest. GDG members were reminded of confidentiality requirements at each meeting. Three GDG meetings were held during the guideline development process: two in-person meetings in Geneva in 2019 and one virtual meeting in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Subgroup sessions were held to accommodate different time zones, with only the GDG Chair, GRADE Methodologist, and two WHO Secretariat members attending all sessions. Consensus was defined as agreement among all GDG members, with a protocol for voting in case of disagreement, though voting was not required for any key questions. The guideline development process was informed by three key questions: (1) the effectiveness of comprehensive SHS in improving health outcomes or increasing health service coverage for school-age children and adolescents, including economic evaluations; (2) the acceptability of comprehensive SHS to stakeholders such as students, parents, teachers, and policymakers; and (3) the content of comprehensive SHS in different contexts. Seven broad health areas were defined: positive health and development, unintentional injury, violence, sexual and reproductive health (including HIV), communicable diseases, noncommunicable diseases (including sensory functions, physical disability, oral health, nutrition, and physical activity), and mental health (including substance use and self-harm). Comprehensive SHS are defined as services that include interventions from at least four of these seven health areas, distinguishing them from narrowly focused health interventions delivered in schools, such as vaccination campaigns. The guideline also defines seven types of SHS activities: health promotion, health education, screening, preventive interventions, clinical assessment, health services management, and others. The guideline was developed following WHO standard procedures, involving systematic reviews and evidence assessment. Given the diversity of SHS combinations and the novelty of this global guidance, only one overarching recommendation was provided, addressing the effectiveness and acceptability of SHS. Practical information on specific interventions for comprehensive SHS implementation is included, though these interventions were not evaluated through the standard WHO guideline recommendation process. The systematic review process identified 20 reviews demonstrating the effectiveness of SHS across various health domains, including depression, anxiety, obesity, oral health, and sleep. Two new systematic reviews were conducted to assess the effectiveness and acceptability of comprehensive SHS. The GRADE approach was used to evaluate the quality of evidence, and the WHO-INTEGRATE tool was considered but not used due to lack of prior experience with it in guideline development. The systematic reviews included only SHS delivered or supervised by health workers and excluded services provided solely by trained teachers. Interventions had to include at least one clinical strategy, such as screening, preventive interventions (e.g., immunizations), or clinical assessment, with or without additional health promotion or education activities.
